<reason>CON built the sharpest reframe of the debate — that PRO's own "regulate the product, not the process" principle argues against a technique-defined lane, and that a technique-neutral risk-based framework with published low-risk eligibility criteria captures every efficiency PRO wants without privileging a molecular label. That kept the "what does the separate category add?" burden live all the way through, and CON's pressure Q2 was the best single question of the round. But CON never contested the empirical anchor: PRO's working notification-plus-escalation model (Japan, Argentina, Brazil) and the mutagenesis inconsistency. Forced by PRO's Q2, CON conceded that conventional and mutagenized crops must also affirmatively support their lighter treatment with evidence — a coherent but implementation-heavy answer that PRO immediately monetised: CON's symmetry is bought by reopening ordinary plant-breeding regulation, while PRO's default is already operating. PRO also closed the loop that CON's "binding published eligibility criteria" for low-risk edits is, in substance, streamlined rules distinct from the GMO dossier wearing a neutral badge — so the residual dispute narrows to who bears the default burden, where PRO's cassava/teff breeder framing has real bite and CON's "public funding can assist" is thinner. PRO also answered the pressure questions with clean A1:/A2: labels and conceded the right things (breeders fund targeted testing when hazard is plausible), which made its lane look like triage rather than deregulation. Execution costs against PRO: one turn clipped for over-length, mis-numbered references to CON's case, and a premature "went unanswered" charge about a question CON had not yet had a substantive turn to answer. Those trim the margin but do not overturn PRO's cleaner comparative story and more concrete stakes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q2 ("which requirement would your pathway remove that couldn't also be waived technique-neutrally?") forced PRO's best moment: PRO named presumption-of-novelty burdens (confined-release permits, event-specific dossiers, traceability duties) and answered with "a waiver you must litigate is not a waiver — defaults are gatekeeping, not paperwork." CON's counter (publish binding criteria, no litigation) was strong, but PRO's closing rejoinder — that published low-risk criteria for edited crops just is the motion, and CON's alternative otherwise requires reopening conventional breeding regulation — left PRO ahead on the decisive clash.</best_rebuttal>
